draft.title: The Commonwealth Constitution
card: The Commonwealth Constitution is the document that set up Australia's federal system in 1901. It is the highest law for the national government.
It says how federal parliament is made up: the Crown, the Senate and the House of Representatives.
It lists the subjects the Commonwealth Parliament may make laws on, such as trade and commerce, defence and immigration. Parliament cannot make laws outside its listed powers.
It also shares power between the Commonwealth and the states. The states keep their own parliaments and their own law-making powers.
draft.remember: The Constitution builds federal parliament, limits what it may legislate on and shares power with the states.

a.q: Which statement best describes a role of the Commonwealth Constitution?
opts: It sets out the subjects federal parliament may legislate on
It lists every offence that a person can be charged with
It decides each case brought before the federal courts
It sets the policies that a government must follow
a.why: The Constitution gives federal parliament a list of subjects it may make laws on. It does not list offences, because those are made in ordinary laws. It does not decide cases, because courts do that.
a.clue: Think about what limits the reach of federal parliament.

b.q: A federal bill is proposed on a subject the Constitution does not give the Commonwealth power over. What does this show about the Constitution?
opts: It limits what federal parliament may make laws on
It lets federal parliament pass any law it wants
It gives the states control over the lower house
It stops the states from having their own parliaments
b.why: The Constitution lists the subjects federal parliament may legislate on, so parliament cannot go beyond them. The states keep their own parliaments, so the last option is wrong.
b.clue: Parliament's powers come from a list.

a.best: It sets out the subjects federal parliament may legislate on

b.best: It limits what federal parliament may make laws on

problems.detail: The scenario only says a bill is 'proposed' on a subject outside Commonwealth power, and a proposal on its own shows nothing about the Constitution. The stem should say what follows, for example that such a law would be invalid or could be struck down, so the link to the Constitution limiting parliament is clear.

b.q: Federal parliament passes a law on a subject the Constitution does not give it. The law could be found invalid. What does this show about the Constitution?
opts: It limits what federal parliament may make laws on
It lets parliament pass any law that both houses agree to
It gives the states control over federal parliament
It stops the states from making their own laws
b.why: The Constitution lists the subjects federal parliament may legislate on, so a law outside that list can be found invalid. Both houses agreeing is not enough, because the law must still fit within the listed powers. The states keep their own law-making powers, so the last option is wrong.
b.clue: Ask why a law passed by parliament could still fail.
